finding.headline: At 53, you can contribute more to a 401(k) now, and the catch-up limit rises at 60.
details: For 2027, the 401(k) catch-up limit for people 50 and over is $8,500, so you can contribute up to $34,000 a year.
At ages 60 to 63, the catch-up limit rises to $11,750 for plans that offer it.
Your plan to retire at 72 means Social Security benefits grow until age 70, and you can sign up for Medicare at 65 to avoid higher costs later.

finding.headline: You have no children or pets, so family costs are zero for this plan.
details: Your home loan ends in 2041, and housing costs fall by $3,700 a year then.
Once retired, basic needs are about $24,200 a year, or $2,017 a month. Health before Medicare is $10,000 a year, and a new roof around 2030 costs $20,000.

finding.headline: About 19% of your pay goes to tax now, and retirement tax looks very low.
details: Of your $55,000 pay, federal tax is $4,352, state tax is $1,688, and payroll tax is $4,208. Together that is $10,248 in total tax, leaving $44,752 after tax.
All of your savings are in taxable and cash accounts right now, so you draw on those first. In retirement, your estimated tax is about $148 a year, and no pension or part-time pay is counted.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Talk with a tax professional before you change how you save or withdraw.

finding.headline: The spending goal lasted in 0 of 100 scenarios, so the current plan does not hold up.
details: The goal is $42,000 a year. The safe amount is $25,800 a year, which covers the basics in 100 of 100 scenarios, but not the full goal. The gap is $16,200 a year.
The plan kept is the simple plan: stocks at 110 minus your age. Savings are $29,200 in cash with no retirement accounts, so the money runs out in all 100 scenarios by age 92.
Markets are uncertain, and these results are not promises. Lowering the goal, saving more before age 72, or getting help with the credit card and roof costs could change the outcome.

finding.headline: You can count on $25,800 a year: $24,200 for basics and $1,600 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $24,200 a year.
Your spending goal of $42,000 a year lasts in 0 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $2,148 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $22,600 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $28,000 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 92. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
